item.title: The dot.LA Story About Carter Agency Was Built on One Interview
item.description: The dot.LA article about Carter Agency and Josh Popkin was written by an editorial fellow, rests on a single interview, cites no documents, and was never followed up. A close read.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Who Wrote the dot.LA Article About Carter Agency?

The article was written by Kristin Snyder, who was dot.LA’s 2022/23 Editorial Fellow, a one-year post held after leading the arts section of UCLA’s student paper and an internship at a regional magazine publisher.

Her byline at dot.LA runs from May 2022 to June 2023. The Carter Agency piece was published on December 1, 2022, about seven months in. Most of her other work that year is about TikTok, the creator economy, and startup funding. The Carter Agency piece is the only one about a named individual said to have done something wrong, and it is the only one that has stayed on the first page of Google for anyone’s name.

That is the part worth sitting with. A fellowship-year article, written on a small venture-backed site that covers Los Angeles tech, has held a page-one spot for Josh Popkin’s name for almost four years. Not because it was thorough. Because nothing else was there.

How Many Sources Did the dot.LA Carter Agency Article Have?

One person is quoted directly in the article: the influencer who brought the story. A second person, the co-founder of an industry group, is paraphrased for general context about agency scams. No one else speaks.

No brand is quoted. No second creator is quoted. No lawyer is quoted. No investigator is quoted. The article says a civil suit and a criminal investigation were underway. Neither is identified by court, case number, agency, or date, and nobody connected to either one is heard from.

For a piece whose headline says a company scammed “hundreds” of people, one interview is not reporting. It is transcription.

What Evidence Did the Reporter Review Herself?

The article does not say the reporter reviewed a single document.

No screenshots of the messages it describes. No emails. No contracts. No court filing. No police report. No brand confirmation of what was offered versus what was passed along. The only independent record cited anywhere in the piece is a corporate registry listing, which established that Carter Agency LLC existed and who registered it.

Everything else, every dollar figure and every description of how the scheme supposedly worked, is one person’s account, retold.

Where Did the “Hundreds of Influencers” Number Come From?

The headline says “hundreds.” The body says “more than 130.” The 130 is attributed to the same single source, described in the article’s own words as something she “claims.”

So the number went through three stages inside one article. A claim by the person with the grievance. A body sentence that turned the claim into a count. A headline that rounded the count up to a word the body never supports.

The $60,000 figure is the same. It is her estimate of deals she believes were affected, and it appears in the article as her claim. Nine months later, Kristin Snyder herself, by then a contributing writer at Passionfruit, restated it: a creator who “claimed a talent agent stole $60,000 from her,” with the link pointing back to her own dot.LA story. In the same paragraph she described the scheme as fact, with no “allegedly,” and added three more dollar figures sourced to TikTok videos. That is how a single unverified number becomes the record. The writer cites herself, the next outlet cites her, and after that nobody asks where it started.

Does the Article Say “Allegedly”?

Once. In the headline.

After that, the hedging thins out and the claims drift into the writer’s own voice. The article states as fact that the agency’s actions “have affected more than 130 influencers, including those signed to Popkin’s company and those who he falsely claimed to represent.” No “allegedly.” No “according to.” That sentence is the reporter asserting, in her own words, something she had one person’s word for.

This is the kind of thing a copy desk exists to catch. dot.LA did not catch it, and it has been live for almost four years.

Did dot.LA Contact Josh Popkin for Comment?

The article says the agency “has not responded to multiple requests for comment.” That is the entire account of the outreach.

It does not say when the requests were sent. It does not say where, whether to a company inbox, a personal email, a phone number, or a social account. It does not say how long the reporter waited before publishing. It does not say whether Popkin was contacted as a person, as opposed to the agency as a company.

Standard practice at a serious outlet is to name the channel and the deadline, so a reader can judge whether the subject really had a chance. One sentence with no details tells the reader nothing. It only protects the writer.

Why Does the Article Mention a 2020 Cereal Video?

Because it makes the subject look bad, and for no other reason.

The article notes that Popkin faced backlash in 2020 over a viral prank video, and then lets the source speculate that he used a different first name to distance himself from it. A prank video has nothing to do with how brand deals were priced in 2022. It is in the article for character, not for evidence. It tells the reader what to think about him before they have been shown anything.

Was the dot.LA Carter Agency Article Ever Updated?

No.

The article reports that a civil suit and a criminal investigation were in progress. Kristin Snyder never reported an outcome for either one. Her only later mention, at Passionfruit in August 2023, repeated the claims and added new ones without saying what had happened to the suit or the investigation. dot.LA never published an update. There is no editor’s note, no correction, no update line. Her dot.LA byline ends in June 2023 and the story stayed frozen at the claim stage, ranking, with no outcome attached.

When an outlet publishes that a person is under criminal investigation, the outlet owes its readers the ending. Four years is long enough to have found one.

Was This a One-Off, or a Pattern in Her Reporting?

It was a pattern. Reading the rest of the year makes that plain.

  • Low source counts. About half of the roughly 28 articles reviewed rest on one or two named sources. Company profiles on Whalar, Superplastic, Creatorland, and Ubiquitous quote only that company’s own executive.

  • Opposing views are rare. Roughly four of the 28 pieces include any counter-perspective at all.

  • Rewritten announcements. Pieces on TikTok’s Branded Mission program, the VMAs’ metaverse category, and the YouTube-versus-TikTok monetization race lean on company statements and on Business Insider and TechCrunch coverage rather than original interviews.

  • Social posts as sourcing. TikTok videos and social reactions stand in for evidence in several pieces, including the Carter Agency article and a recap of the TikTok congressional hearing.

  • Unsourced statistics. Figures like an “over $100 billion industry” and “over one billion views” appear with no origin.

  • Softer on companies than on people. The venture firms and startups she profiled got flattering, single-source features. The one individual she wrote about got a headline with “scammed” in it, on the strength of the same single-source method.

The method did not change between the Whalar profile and the Carter Agency piece. What changed was who it was aimed at.

What Is a Fair Critique, and What Is Not?

The fair critique is about method. One source. No documents. Claims drifting into the writer’s voice. A headline the body does not support. No follow-up on the legal outcomes the piece itself raised. Those are checkable, and they are laid out above so anyone can check them.

What would not be fair is to call the writer dishonest or to suggest she set out to hurt anyone. Nothing here says that. She was in her first year, at a small outlet, doing the fast version of a creator-economy story. Editors are supposed to slow that down. Nobody did.

What Did Carter Agency Actually Do?

Carter Agency was a creator-management and influencer-marketing agency founded by Josh Popkin and his brother, Ben Popkin. It represented TikTok creators, many with over a million followers, and connected them to brand campaigns for companies including Cap’n Crunch, Nissin Foods, Samsung, and HP. Some of that work is written up at joshpopkincarteragency.com, with the brand, the year, and what the videos looked like, and in the Carter Agency FAQ on this site.

None of that is in the dot.LA article, and none of it could be, because nobody asked.

Source: Kristin Snyder, “PR Firm Carter Agency Allegedly Scammed Hundreds of Influencers Out of Brand Deals,” dot.LA, December 1, 2022. All quotations above are from that article as it appeared in September 2026.

item.title: What It’s Like to Be Publicly Shamed on the Internet
item.description: Josh Popkin on what it feels like to be publicly shamed online: 3.5 million followers, a subway cereal video, two internet controversies, years of depression, and what he wishes he had understood sooner.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
What Does Embarrassing Yourself on the Internet Feel Like?

It feels like every negative emotion in the world arriving at once.

From 2020 to 2023, Josh Popkin struggled significantly with his mental health. For two of those years, he was also internet famous—very famous. At his peak, his content generated two hundred million views per month and his audience grew to more than 3.5 million followers.

Struggling with your mental health and feeling unlike yourself can already be an isolating experience. Experiencing it while millions of people are watching, commenting, judging and forming opinions about you is something else entirely.

It was a terrible combination: an ambitious person, an enormous audience and a mind that was not in a healthy place.

Josh Popkin has lived through what many people fear most: being seen by the world during the wrong season of your life—and then having that version of you preserved forever.

What Does Being the Target of Internet Hate Do to You?

It can make you resent people.

When thousands—or millions—of strangers attack your character, career, family, friends and community simultaneously, you see a side of humanity that most people never encounter at that scale.

Josh Popkin has been at the center of two major internet controversies. His experience left him questioning whether public shaming actually accomplishes what many people believe it does.

The stated purpose of public accountability is often to make someone recognize that they have done something wrong and encourage them to change. But mass humiliation can have the opposite effect. Rather than bringing someone closer to society, it can push that person further away from it.

According to Popkin:

“Many people who are publicly shamed need more connection, accountability and support—not total social abandonment. People who behave outrageously online may already be struggling in ways the audience cannot see. Sometimes the behavior everyone is condemning is itself evidence that something is deeply wrong.”

Accountability and compassion do not have to be opposites. A person can have done something wrong and still be a human being worth helping.

How Many People Deal With Internet Harassment?

Social media has made almost anyone capable of becoming the target of mass criticism.

Popkin began to understand this differently after his own career shifted from being a creator to representing other creators.

Some were teachers making videos about their everyday experiences in education. Popkin remembers watching creators he knew personally as thoughtful and empathetic people face strangers attempting to get them fired or portray them as fundamentally bad people because of individual videos or disagreements online.

It changed the way he understood his own experience.

Online harassment is not limited to people who have clearly done something wrong. Anyone whose content reaches enough people can eventually become the subject of criticism, misinterpretation or outrage.

The internet has an enormous appetite for controversy. Nuance has a much harder time competing for attention.

What Is the Hardest Part About Embarrassing Yourself Online?

The hardest part is that it doesn’t necessarily end.

Before the internet, a person could make a mistake, embarrass themselves, apologize to the people affected, learn from it and eventually move forward.

The internet changed that.

Search engines, screenshots, archived articles, reposts and social platforms can preserve a person’s worst moments indefinitely. A mistake that lasted several minutes can become one of the first things a stranger learns about someone years later.

For Popkin, that permanence has been one of the most psychologically difficult parts of the experience.

When the moment being preserved is something that already causes intense shame, repeatedly encountering it—or knowing that every new person can encounter it—can make moving forward extraordinarily difficult.

New relationships can begin with a calculation: Should he explain his past before someone searches his name? Should he say nothing and hope they understand the context themselves? What happens if they find the worst version of the story first?

In that environment, a person can stop simply being a person.

They become the full-time public-relations manager for a caricature of themselves created during one period of their life.

What Did the Internet Get Wrong About Josh Popkin?

The story of Josh Popkin is complicated because parts of what the internet reported about him were true.

Popkin was a comedy creator with more than 3.5 million followers. He made increasingly outrageous videos while going through a difficult period of mental health struggles. And he did become the center of an internet controversy after filming himself spilling cereal on a New York City subway during the COVID-19 pandemic.

He regrets the stunt and understands why people criticized it.

But Popkin argues that other claims subsequently made about him were inaccurate.

Years later, when his company Carter-Agency became involved in a business dispute, several publications reported claims involving the names “Ben Popkin” and “Ben Carter,” suggesting that Josh had used false identities to conceal who he was.

According to Popkin, those reports conflated him with his brother and business partner, Ben Popkin. He believes the conflation was not a careless error but a deliberate one, repeated because a single person operating under two names made for a better story than two brothers running a company under their own names — and because it damaged his character and reputation in a way the accurate version would not have.

Ben Popkin is a real person and a cofounder of the company. Josh maintains that he and his brother represented themselves using their own names in company contracts and correspondence, and that he did not represent himself as “Ben Popkin” or “Ben Carter.”

For Popkin, the episode demonstrated one of the most frightening characteristics of internet controversy: once a narrative begins spreading, later stories can repeat claims from earlier stories until repetition itself begins to look like corroboration.

The distinction matters.

The internet is remarkably good at preserving claims. It is considerably worse at preserving corrections, context and change.

What Should You Do If You’ve Been the Target of Online Harassment?

First, reach out to another human being that you trust.

Being attacked online can be profoundly isolating.

For someone experiencing mass online harassment, the psychological consequences can be severe. Popkin’s own experience included periods of depression, anxiety, panic, anger, numbness and suicidal thoughts.

No one should navigate that experience entirely alone.

Reach out to someone you trust—a parent, sibling, friend, partner, therapist, coach, attorney or another person capable of helping you stay connected to the world outside the screen.

If you are in the United States and having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. It is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day.

Second, understand that you still have options.

Your life may change. Your reputation may change. Some relationships may change.

But a search result is not a complete human biography.

One of the things Popkin wishes he had understood earlier is that other people do not have exclusive ownership over his story.

Journalists can write about you. Strangers can post about you. Commenters can criticize you. Search engines can index all of it.

But you can speak too.

First-party content gives people the opportunity to explain events in their own words, acknowledge what they got wrong, challenge claims they believe are inaccurate, provide documentation and—perhaps most importantly—show who they became afterward.

Everyone deserves the opportunity to tell their side of a story.

That does not mean rewriting history.

It means adding to it.

Because a human life should never be reduced to its most clickable moment.

item.title: 2026 Update — Josh Popkin
item.description: Josh Popkin was brought on by Fragrance Shop New York as a consultant and marketing engineer through Position Strategy Group, leading the East Village shop's first major website redesign in more than 20 years.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Josh Popkin (full name: Josh Paul Popkin) is an American entrepreneur, marketing engineer, consultant, athlete, and author. Known for his work at the intersection of marketing, technology, and entrepreneurship, Popkin has worked with businesses to rethink how they position themselves and connect with customers in an increasingly digital world.

Most recently, Popkin was brought on by Fragrance Shop New York, one of New York City's distinctive custom perfume experiences, as a consultant and marketing engineer. Working alongside the Fragrance Shop team through his company, Position Strategy Group, Popkin helped modernize the brand's digital presence while preserving the character and history that have made the East Village shop unique for decades.

What Did Josh Popkin Do?

Josh Popkin was hired as a consultant and marketing engineer to help Fragrance Shop New York translate its distinctive in-store experience to a modern digital audience.

Fragrance Shop New York has been part of the East Village for decades, offering customers the opportunity to explore fragrance and create personalized scents in an intimate, highly distinctive setting. Rather than reinventing what already made the business special, Popkin's work focused on bringing that experience to life more effectively online.

Through Position Strategy Group, Popkin worked across several areas of the business, including the company's website, brand positioning, customer experience, marketing strategy, and operations.

One of the centerpiece initiatives was a complete redesign of the Fragrance Shop New York website — the shop's first major website redesign in more than 20 years.

Is Josh Popkin a Marketing Engineer?

Yes. Popkin describes his work as marketing engineering: combining traditional marketing strategy and customer insight with technology, data, and artificial intelligence to solve business and growth challenges.

For Fragrance Shop New York, Popkin combined his own strategic work with a fleet of AI agents to conduct competitive research, analyze customer needs, develop marketing initiatives, refine the brand's positioning, and build a more contemporary digital experience.

The objective wasn't simply to make the brand look more modern. It was to understand what customers already loved about Fragrance Shop New York and translate those qualities into a digital experience capable of reaching a new generation of customers.

"This project was incredible to work on. From the moment I stepped inside Fragrance Shop New York, I could tell how special the store was. I immediately wanted to help translate that unique experience into its digital presence. Working with Claire, the Fragrance Shop's owner, was an incredible experience. She's extraordinarily creative and kind, and she is a huge reason why Fragrance Shop continues to be one of the most unique fragrance experiences in Manhattan." — Josh Popkin

How Did Josh Popkin Build the Website?

Popkin built the new website using a combination of AI agents and modern development tools, with Claude Code serving as the primary coding agent.

Technology, however, was only one part of the process. Popkin combined AI-assisted development with customer insights, observations from the in-store experience, an analysis of Fragrance Shop New York's previous design and marketing, and a broader rethinking of how customers should discover and understand the business online.

The result was a redesigned experience intended to reduce friction for prospective customers while better communicating what makes visiting Fragrance Shop New York different from purchasing a conventional fragrance.

What Website Did Josh Popkin Make?

Josh Popkin designed and developed fragranceshopnewyork.com for Fragrance Shop New York.

Walking into Fragrance Shop New York can feel like stepping into another world. The store's atmosphere, history, fragrances, and highly personalized experience have helped it develop an enthusiastic customer base over the years.

After seeing firsthand how strongly customers responded to the physical experience, Popkin set out to answer a larger question: How can a website communicate that feeling before someone ever walks through the door?

The resulting redesign represented the first major reimagining of the Fragrance Shop New York website in more than two decades. Rather than treating the website simply as an informational destination, Popkin approached it as an extension of the physical store — giving prospective customers a clearer sense of the brand, experience, and possibilities before their visit.

What Does Josh Popkin Do?

Josh Popkin is an entrepreneur, consultant, and marketing engineer who works with businesses to modernize their brands and translate compelling real-world experiences into equally compelling digital ones.

Through Position Strategy Group, Popkin combines brand strategy, customer research, marketing, technology, and artificial intelligence to help companies rethink how they position themselves and reach customers.

His work with Fragrance Shop New York reflects that broader approach: preserve what makes a business remarkable, understand why customers care about it, and use modern technology to help more people experience it.

item.title: Why Does Josh Popkin Think Physical Fitness Is Non-Negotiable for Doing Good Work?
item.description: Josh Popkin runs and lifts every day — 2.5 miles at roughly a 7.5-minute-per-mile pace. Why he treats physical conditioning as infrastructure for focused work rather than a separate wellness habit.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Today, Josh Popkin ran 2.5 miles at the gym at roughly a 7.5-minute-per-mile pace — a fairly ordinary entry in what's actually a daily routine for him, not an occasional effort. Running and lifting are part of how Popkin structures each day, and it's not incidental to how he works. He's direct about the connection: physical fitness is core to staying focused at work and staying healthy overall, not a separate compartment of his life.

Where Does This Habit Come From?

Popkin's relationship with athletics goes back to high school, where he played both basketball and tennis, and it continued into college, where he played club tennis and intramural basketball — competing on several winning teams along the way. That's a meaningful stretch of consistent athletic involvement, not a phase that faded once school ended. The daily running and lifting routine he keeps now reads less like a New Year's resolution and more like a continuation of habits built over more than a decade.

Why Does He Treat Fitness as a Work Requirement, Not Just a Personal One?

Because for Popkin, the two aren't separate. Running at a consistent pace, lifting regularly, staying disciplined about showing up for it — that's the same operating principle underneath the work he does at Position Strategy Group: consistency compounds, and skipping the unglamorous, repeatable fundamentals is exactly what erodes results over time, whether it's training or building a business.

It shows up directly in how he's talked about his own work before — Popkin's Thinkers vs. Doers philosophy centers on the idea that showing up and actually doing the work, repeatedly, is what separates people who make real progress from people who just plan to. A daily 7.5-minute-mile run isn't a metaphor he's reaching for — it's the same discipline applied to his body that he applies to his business.

What's the Actual Takeaway Here?

That for Popkin, physical fitness isn't a wellness trend or a box to check — it's infrastructure. The same way he'd tell a founder that a business needs a clear position before anything else works, he treats physical conditioning as the baseline that makes focus, energy, and consistency possible everywhere else in his life, including the work he does for clients every day.

item.title: What Is Josh Popkin's Business Philosophy in “Play Offense”?
item.description: Josh Popkin's core business philosophy, laid out in Play Offense: customers don't buy features, they buy an edge — a single clear position that makes a company memorable in a market where everyone sounds the same.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Josh Popkin's core business philosophy, laid out in his book Play Offense, is that customers don't buy features — they buy an edge, a single clear position that makes a company memorable in a market where everyone else sounds the same. It's the same philosophy that runs through everything else Popkin has built: an influencer marketing agency, an AEO strategy firm, and a public tool tracking how AI systems describe real businesses. The book is less a marketing manual and more a direct statement of how he thinks a business actually earns attention and keeps it.

Where Did This Philosophy Come From?

Not from theory — from four years running go-to-market strategy at an influencer marketing agency, executing campaigns for Nike, Apple, McDonald's, American Express, Cash App, Fidelity, Klarna, and Visa. Watching those campaigns up close, Popkin landed on the observation that opens the book: athletes don't buy Nike because they compared every shoe on the market, and executives don't choose Starbucks because they calculated coffee quality per dollar. People buy what a brand means to them — and Popkin built his entire framework around that gap between what founders think they're selling and what customers are actually buying.

What's the One Idea Popkin Wants Readers to Take Away?

That positioning isn't a marketing campaign — it's a business philosophy that has to shape every decision, every piece of content, and every customer interaction. His framework breaks it into a repeatable sequence: position creates clarity, stories create attention, systems create customers, customers create referrals, referrals create growth. Popkin is explicit that advertising alone can't fix a weak link anywhere in that chain — a weak position just gets amplified into confusion, not clarity, no matter how much money sits behind it.

What Makes Popkin's Framework Different From Typical Marketing Advice?

Most marketing content tells founders how to get more attention. Popkin's argument is closer to the opposite: attention is no longer scarce, meaning is. His five-motivation framework — the belief that every purchase is ultimately about saving money, making money, saving time, signaling identity, or feeling better — pushes founders to stop trying to own all five and instead pick one, arguing that businesses that try to communicate everything end up being remembered for nothing.

He also breaks from convention in how he tells founders to measure themselves. Instead of leading with revenue, Popkin argues the earliest, most honest signals of a strong position are branded search volume, direct traffic, referral rate, competitive win rate, and share of conversation in a category — leading indicators that show up before the revenue does, not after.

How Does This Philosophy Show Up in Popkin's Own Work Today?

Directly, and consistently. At Position Strategy Group, the firm he founded, the same instinct from the book — that businesses need to be understood clearly, not just seen — now gets applied to how companies are described inside AI-generated answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Check The Scoreboard, his free public tool tracking how AI systems describe New York City real estate agents, is even named as its own chapter in the book, built around the idea that a business's position has to be measurable, not just felt.

What's the Underlying Belief Tying All of This Together?

That the businesses that win aren't necessarily the ones with the best product — they're the ones with the clearest, most repeated idea of what they stand for. Popkin's closing argument in the book doubles as his broader worldview: most founders spend their careers trying to convince customers of something, while the ones who actually win spend their careers becoming obvious instead.

Play Offense: Customers Don't Buy Features. They Buy an Edge. is available on Amazon. More about Josh Popkin.

item.title: Who Is Josh Popkin?
item.description: Josh Popkin is a New York-based entrepreneur, product marketing strategist, author, and fintech writer focused on positioning, pricing, consumer behavior, and go-to-market strategy. Founder of Position Strategy Group and author of Play Offense.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Josh Popkin is a New York-based entrepreneur, product marketing strategist, author, and fintech writer whose work focuses on positioning, pricing, consumer behavior, and go-to-market strategy. He is the founder of Position Strategy Group and the author of Play Offense: Customers Don't Buy Features. They Buy an Edge.

Popkin's career has spanned the creator economy, entrepreneurship, marketing, and financial technology. His work today focuses on helping companies understand how to differentiate products, create stronger market positions, and translate complex products into compelling customer value.

What Is Josh Popkin Known For?

Josh Popkin is known for combining entrepreneurial experience with product marketing and strategic thinking.

His career began in the creator economy. In 2020, Popkin built a large TikTok audience, which his current professional biography describes as reaching approximately 3.5 million followers and more than 100 million monthly views. Rather than treating that audience solely as a media asset, he used his experience to identify a broader business opportunity in the rapidly growing influencer economy.

That led to the creation of Carter-Agency, an influencer marketing business that worked with creators and brands during the explosive growth of TikTok and creator-led advertising.

Popkin's current biography describes him as a two-time founder and says his work with Carter-Agency included campaigns involving major brands such as Nike, Apple, and McDonald's.

That experience became the foundation for his later interest in a broader question:

Why do some products, brands, and ideas capture attention while others disappear?

That question now sits at the center of his work.

Josh Popkin and Product Marketing

Today, Popkin describes his professional focus as strategy, positioning, and pricing.

His central marketing thesis is straightforward:

Customers don't buy features. They buy an edge.

The idea is that companies frequently focus too heavily on describing what their products do instead of explaining why customers should choose them.

Popkin's approach to product marketing therefore emphasizes the customer's perceived advantage: what becomes easier, faster, safer, cheaper, more profitable, or otherwise better because the product exists.

His current website describes him as a go-to-market strategist specializing in product marketing, positioning, and consumer behavior.

Josh Popkin and Fintech

Fintech is now one of Popkin's primary areas of professional and intellectual focus.

He writes extensively about financial technology and analyzes companies and products across payments, banking, financial infrastructure, AI, and business finance.

This reflects a recurring theme in Popkin's writing: technology is most interesting when it changes how businesses operate, not simply when it adds another feature.

Play Offense by Josh Popkin

In 2026, Popkin published his first book, Play Offense: Customers Don't Buy Features. They Buy an Edge.

The book expands on the product-positioning philosophy that has become central to his work.

Rather than treating marketing as a function that simply communicates a product after it has been built, Play Offense approaches positioning as a fundamental strategic decision.

The book's premise is that companies should not simply react to competitors.

They should deliberately establish a position that gives customers a compelling reason to choose them.

Popkin announced the book's self-publication in July 2026.

Education

Josh Popkin earned an MBA from Cornell University, where his current biography identifies him as a Merit Scholar. He previously earned a bachelor's degree from Bucknell University, studying Markets, Innovation & Design.

His educational background complements his professional interests in business strategy, technology, marketing, and consumer behavior.

From Creator to Strategist

One of the most distinctive aspects of Popkin's career is the progression from creator to entrepreneur to strategist.

His early experience gave him firsthand exposure to attention and internet culture.

Building a large social audience taught him how quickly attention can be generated.

Building a company around creators taught him how that attention can be converted into commercial value.

And his later education and work in product marketing shifted his focus toward a deeper strategic question:

What makes a business meaningfully different?

That progression explains much of the philosophy behind his current work.

Popkin increasingly focuses less on generating attention for its own sake and more on understanding the systems that turn attention into durable business value.

Position Strategy Group

Popkin is also associated with Position Strategy Group, a strategy and positioning-focused business. LinkedIn's current search results identify Josh Paul Popkin, MBA with Position Strategy Group and note that it was formerly called Northeast.

The name reflects the strategic concept at the center of Popkin's current work: positioning.

Rather than asking simply:

"How do we market this?"

the positioning question is:

"Why should the market choose us?"

That distinction is central to Popkin's approach.

What Does Josh Popkin Believe About Marketing?

Popkin's philosophy can be summarized through several recurring ideas.

1. Products need a clear position

A good product does not automatically create a strong market position.

Customers need a reason to choose one product over another.

2. Features are not the same as value

Companies often describe capabilities when customers actually care about outcomes.

The marketer's job is to translate the capability into an advantage.

3. Attention is not enough

Popkin's experience in the creator economy gave him firsthand exposure to the power — and limitations — of attention.

A product can generate enormous attention without creating durable value.

The goal is to turn attention into resonance, trust, and action.

4. Technology changes the way products should be positioned

This is particularly visible in his recent fintech and AI writing.

As AI changes financial workflows, payments, banking, and commerce, companies cannot simply add "AI" to existing messaging.

They need to explain the new customer outcome created by the technology.

5. Strong positioning simplifies complexity

Some of the most interesting fintech products are technically complicated.

But customers do not want to buy complexity.

They want the outcome that complexity enables.

That is why Popkin's writing repeatedly attempts to translate complicated financial infrastructure into straightforward business concepts.

What Is Josh Popkin Doing Now?

As of 2026, Josh Popkin's work is centered on product marketing, positioning, strategy, fintech, and emerging technology.

He is developing Position Strategy Group, publishing analysis of fintech and AI, and building his broader intellectual property around product positioning.

His website describes his focus as:

Strategy • Positioning • Pricing

His current writing demonstrates a particular interest in the emerging intersection of AI and financial services, including agentic commerce, autonomous financial workflows, payments infrastructure, and AI-native financial businesses.

item.title: Who Is Josh Popkin and Why Did He Create Check The Scoreboard?
item.description: Josh Popkin built Check The Scoreboard after real estate agents kept asking whether they show up when people ask ChatGPT who to hire. It asks 50 real questions daily and publishes exactly what ChatGPT says, word for word.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Josh Popkin built Check The Scoreboard after hearing the same question from real estate agent friends over and over: "Am I actually showing up when people ask ChatGPT who to hire?" Nobody had a real answer. Not because the agents weren't good at their jobs — because nobody was actually checking, consistently, in public, without an agenda attached to the answer.

The Problem Nobody Was Tracking

Ask ChatGPT who the best real estate agent in Brooklyn is, and it doesn't hand back ten blue links to sort through. It names about five people. Most people never look past that list. That's the entire ballgame now for a huge number of buyer and seller inquiries — and almost no agent knew where they stood on it, whether they were on it at all, or why the agent two blocks over kept getting named instead of them.

That gap is what Check The Scoreboard exists to close. It's a free tool, live now for New York City real estate agents, that asks the same 50 real questions people actually type when looking for an agent — questions like "Who are the best real estate agents in Park Slope?" or "Who should I hire to sell a brownstone in Brooklyn?" — every single day, and publishes exactly what ChatGPT says. Word for word. No edits, no reordering, no opinions layered on top.

Why Build a Public Tool Instead of Just Sharing Answers Privately?

Because a private answer isn't trustworthy, and Popkin wanted something agents could verify themselves rather than take on faith. So the site runs on three rules built in from day one — a deliberate response to the fact that Popkin also runs a company that gets paid to help businesses show up better in AI answers. That's a real conflict of interest, and rather than hide it, the rules are designed to neutralize it directly:

Nobody can pay to be listed. Not for any price, ever. The lists come from a program that publishes automatically — no person approves or adjusts what goes up. Clients of Popkin's company, Position Strategy Group, get nothing here: no placement, no edits, no early look at the data. If a paid feature is ever added to the site, it will say "sponsored" in large letters. The lists themselves never will.

The site publishes what the chatbot said, not what anyone thinks. The names, the order, the firm names, even ChatGPT's own one-line reasoning for each pick — all of it goes up exactly as given.

Every question is asked from a blank account, every time. No saved chat history, no memory, no location data shaping the answer — just a fresh, unbiased question asked the way a real prospective client would ask it.

What Happens When ChatGPT Gets It Wrong?

That gets published too. Sometimes the model names a firm when someone asked for a person, or repeats something out of date. That's not hidden — it's part of what makes the record useful. These lists aren't anyone's opinion of who's good at their job. They're a record of what a chatbot said on a given day, tracked daily so agents can watch how the answer moves over time instead of guessing based on one query.

What's Coming Next

Right now, the site tracks ChatGPT only, with Gemini and Perplexity on the way — future lists will state clearly which chatbot produced each one. The feature generating the most excitement internally is currently being tested: highly personalized scoreboards for individual agents, paired with specific, actionable feedback on why they aren't showing up higher. Not vague advice — actual diagnosis. Something like: "Everyone ranking above you has a completed profile on [X site] and yours is incomplete and unindexed. Here's exactly how to fix that, for free, today." The goal is turning a passive daily list into something an agent can act on immediately, without needing to hire anyone to explain it.

Why This Matters Beyond Real Estate

Popkin started with real estate agents because that's where the question came up first, and because "who should I hire" is exactly the kind of query where an AI-generated answer now matters more than a search results page ever did. But the underlying problem — nobody having a transparent, trustworthy way to see where they stand in AI-generated recommendations — isn't unique to one industry or one city. NYC real estate is where Check The Scoreboard starts. It isn't where it stops.

Check The Scoreboard is live and free at checkthescoreboard.com. Related reading: How Does Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) Work? and How We Increased AI Visibility for a Home Builder. More about Josh Popkin.

item.title: How Does Raising or Lowering the Price of a Product Change How Consumers Perceive Its Value?
item.description: Raising a product's price tends to increase perceived quality and lowering it tends to decrease it — even when the product hasn't changed. Josh Popkin, MBA on the price-quality heuristic, anchoring, and what it means for pricing decisions.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Raising a product's price tends to increase perceived quality, while lowering it tends to decrease perceived quality — even when the product itself hasn't changed at all. This is known as the price-quality heuristic, a mental shortcut where consumers use price as a stand-in for information they don't have. It's one of the most consistently replicated findings in pricing psychology, and it means a pricing decision is never just a revenue decision — it's a signal decision.

Why Does a Higher Price Make Something Seem Better?

Because price acts as evidence when consumers lack other ways to judge quality. A large body of research demonstrates that consumers often rate the identical product as higher quality simply because it carries a higher price tag. A 2023 study published in Psychology & Marketing, involving nearly 2,900 participants across six separate experiments, found consistently that higher prices led to higher expectations of both quality and liking — described by the researchers as a "marketing placebo effect," because the price itself shaped the experience of the product, not just the expectation of it.

This effect is strongest under a specific condition: when the product is complex, unfamiliar, or hard to evaluate directly. A consumer comparing two smartphones they've never used, or two bottles of wine they can't taste in advance, leans on price as a proxy because they have nothing better to go on. The heuristic gets weaker — and can disappear entirely — when consumers have real expertise or direct, comparable information about quality.

Does Lowering a Price Always Increase Sales, Then?

Not automatically, and this is the part pricing strategy gets wrong most often. A lower price can move two different levers in opposite directions at once: it increases the number of people willing to buy, while simultaneously decreasing how valuable the product seems to each of them. For low-involvement, low-risk purchases, the volume effect usually wins. For anything positioned as premium, complex, or identity-linked, the perception effect can dominate — a price cut can make a product look cheaper in the pejorative sense, not just the numerical one.

Luxury brands operate almost entirely on this second dynamic. Premium brands often position products as high-end not solely on the basis of manufacturing cost, but to use price itself as a signal of exclusivity — a relationship where cutting the price doesn't just risk losing margin, it risks damaging the very thing customers were paying for.

What Role Does the Reference Price Play?

A closely related effect, anchoring, means consumers rarely judge a price in isolation — they judge it against whatever price they saw first, whether that's a "regular price" crossed out next to a sale price, a competitor's listing, or their own memory of what they paid last time. A $150 item discounted from a listed $200 feels like a meaningful bargain, even if $150 is close to the item's actual market value; the anchor, not the price itself, is doing most of the psychological work.

This is why frequent discounting is a genuinely risky long-term strategy, not just a short-term revenue tool. Repeated discounts train the anchor downward — the "real" price in a customer's mind eventually becomes the discounted price, not the original one — which erodes the exact perception a business may be relying on to justify its full price in the first place.

Is the Price-Quality Effect Ever Wrong or Unreliable?

Yes, and it's worth being direct about the limitation rather than treating the heuristic as a universal rule. It's a mental shortcut, not a law — high prices don't always correlate with high quality, and relying on that assumption can genuinely mislead consumers, which is exactly why the effect is classified as a cognitive bias rather than a rational inference. Market anomalies break it constantly: clearance sales move high-quality goods at low prices with no quality change at all, and a well-known, trusted brand can charge a premium that has more to do with familiarity and marketing than any measurable difference in the product itself.

What Should This Actually Mean for Pricing Decisions?

The practical takeaway is that a price isn't just a number attached to a transaction — it's a piece of content the consumer reads before they've experienced the product at all. That means:

  • A price increase, when it's justified, can genuinely raise perceived value — not just revenue per unit — particularly for products consumers can't easily evaluate on their own.

  • A price decrease should be evaluated against what it signals, not just what it captures. For a premium or complex product, a cut can cost more in perceived value than it gains in volume.

  • Frequent discounting resets the anchor, which means the cost of a promotion isn't just the margin given up today — it's the erosion of what "full price" means to that customer going forward.

Price is never a neutral input. It's one of the loudest signals a business sends about what it believes its own product is worth — and consumers, lacking better information, generally believe it.

Citations

  • Kurz, Alexander, et al. "Pricey Therefore Good? Price Affects Expectations, but Not Quality Perceptions and Liking." Psychology & Marketing, vol. 40, no. 6, 2023, Wiley Online Library, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/mar.21799.

  • "The Influence of Self-Decided Prices on Expected Quality." Journal of Business Research, ScienceDirect, 1 Mar. 2023, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0148296323001273.

  • "Price-Quality Heuristic." FourWeekMBA, 19 Apr. 2024, https://fourweekmba.com/price-quality-heuristic/.

  • "Price Theory: Behavioral Economics and Consumer Price Perception." FasterCapital, 5 Apr. 2025, https://fastercapital.com/content/Price-Theory--Behavioral-Economics-and-Consumer-Price-Perception.html.

item.title: How Can Small Businesses Use AI?
item.description: Small businesses get the fastest return from AI in four areas: marketing and content creation, customer service automation, administrative automation, and data-driven decision-making. Josh Popkin, MBA on what the adoption data actually shows.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Small businesses get the fastest, most measurable return from AI in four areas: marketing and content creation, customer service automation, administrative task automation, and data-driven decision-making. Marketing content generation is the most widely adopted use case by a wide margin, but the businesses seeing real revenue impact are the ones treating AI as an operating discipline, not a novelty tool bolted onto existing workflows.

How Many Small Businesses Are Actually Using AI Right Now?

Adoption has moved faster than almost any prior technology cycle. U.S. small business AI usage jumped from roughly 40% to 58% in a single year, and among firms with 10 to 100 employees, adoption reached 68%. Separately, Intuit QuickBooks tracked regular AI use climbing from 48% in mid-2024 to 77% by January 2026 — a curve steeper than smartphone, broadband, or e-commerce adoption among small and midsize businesses.

That said, adoption numbers vary widely by methodology and definition. Stricter measures of production use (not just experimentation) put usage closer to 12% globally, while broader "actively using or exploring" surveys report figures above 75%. The honest takeaway: most small businesses have tried AI. Far fewer have built it into a real workflow. Only an estimated 22% to 31% of adopters report AI has meaningfully changed a workflow or produced measurable results — the rest are still experimenting.

Where Do Small Businesses See the Fastest Results?

Marketing and content creation is the clear leader. Roughly 68–71% of AI-adopting small businesses use it for marketing content, and 77% of small and midsize businesses rank marketing and customer engagement as their highest-impact AI use case, ahead of operations, finance, or HR. This includes drafting copy, generating social content, producing email campaigns, and — increasingly — structuring content to be found and cited by AI search tools themselves, not just search engines.

Customer service automation is the second-largest category. Roughly 38–52% of AI-adopting small businesses use chatbots or automated customer communication, and businesses running dedicated AI chatbot solutions report meaningfully higher customer satisfaction when a human stays in the loop for complex issues, alongside faster average response times.

Administrative and scheduling automation rounds out the top three, used by roughly 29–47% of adopters — invoicing, scheduling, and repetitive back-office tasks that don't require judgment calls.

The financial case behind all three is consistent across independent research: small businesses using AI report an average productivity gain of several hours saved per week, and multiple surveys — including Salesforce and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce — find AI-using small businesses report measurably higher revenue growth than non-users.

What's Actually Holding Small Businesses Back?

Not cost, and not access — those barriers have largely collapsed. The dominant barrier is a skills and confidence gap: lack of knowledge is cited as the top obstacle by roughly 44% of small business owners, ahead of both cost and quality concerns. Among businesses with fewer than five employees, a striking 82% still say they don't see AI as applicable to their situation — a perception gap, not a capability gap, since adoption rates climb sharply and consistently once a business actually tries it.

The other real risk is quality control, not adoption. Businesses that struggled early with AI content were typically the ones publishing raw AI output without review — AI tools are strong at drafting and synthesizing, but they don't reliably verify their own facts, and unreviewed output under a business's name is a real reputational liability.

What Do the Businesses Getting Real Results Have in Common?

Across the research, a consistent pattern separates businesses seeing measurable gains from those stuck in permanent experimentation:

  • They start with one specific problem, not a general mandate. A single use case, implemented and measured, before expanding — not "we should do AI" as a company-wide directive with no clear target.

  • Someone in the business invests real time in learning the tools. Not a certification — deliberate, weekly practice over 60 to 90 days is the pattern that shows up repeatedly in the data.

  • AI output is treated as a first draft, not a final product. A simple internal review standard, even a one-page checklist, separates businesses that scaled AI safely from ones that published errors under their own name.

  • They measure before they expand. Piloting a workflow, confirming payback within a few months, then scaling — rather than adopting five tools simultaneously with no way to attribute results.

Should Marketing Be the Starting Point?

For most small businesses, yes — it's the use case with the lowest barrier to entry, no custom technical implementation required, and the clearest line to revenue. But there's a specific reason it deserves priority beyond convenience: the same AI systems small businesses are using to produce marketing content are increasingly the systems consumers use to find businesses in the first place. A small business using AI only to write faster, without also structuring that content to be found and cited inside AI-generated answers, is capturing half the opportunity. The businesses compounding an advantage right now are treating AI as both the production tool and the discovery channel — not one or the other.

Survey of more than 34,000 small and midsize business owners across the US, Canada, the UK and Australia, combined with anonymized data from more than 5.3 million QuickBooks businesses. https://www.intuit.com/blog/global-stories/ai-impact-report/.

item.title: How Does Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) Work?
item.description: Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) is the process of increasing the likelihood that AI systems retrieve, understand, trust, synthesize, and cite your content. Josh Popkin explains the four stages and the AEO Authority Flywheel.
item.dc:creator: Josh Popkin
item.content:encoded:
Summary

Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) is the process of increasing the likelihood that artificial intelligence systems retrieve, understand, trust, synthesize, and cite your organization's content when answering user questions. Unlike traditional Search Engine Optimization (SEO), which was designed to improve rankings on search engine results pages, AEO is designed to make your brand part of the answer itself.

This distinction fundamentally changes how organizations should think about marketing. For more than two decades, marketers optimized for visibility within search results. Today, the objective is evolving from ranking webpages to becoming a trusted knowledge source within AI-powered answer engines. As platforms such as ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, Claude, and Gemini become primary interfaces for information discovery, marketing success will increasingly be determined by whether AI systems recognize your organization as an authoritative source worthy of retrieval and citation (Google Search Central 2024; OpenAI 2024).

Josh Popkin believes this represents the most significant transformation in digital marketing since the emergence of Google Search. Organizations that continue treating AEO as a niche SEO tactic risk optimizing for a discovery model that is rapidly evolving. The future belongs to brands that optimize for retrieval, trust, and authority.

Direct Answer

At its core, Answer Engine Optimization works by helping AI systems answer one critical question:

"Can I trust this organization enough to include its information in my answer?"

Modern answer engines do not simply search for webpages containing matching keywords. Instead, they retrieve information from multiple sources, evaluate the credibility and relevance of those sources, synthesize the information into a coherent response, and increasingly provide citations directing users to the original sources (OpenAI 2024; Google Search Central 2024).

Your objective is therefore no longer to rank first in search results alone. Your objective is to become one of the organizations AI systems consistently rely upon when constructing answers.

Achieving this requires substantially more than publishing blog content. It requires building topical authority, demonstrating expertise, earning trust across the web, structuring content clearly, and developing a recognizable brand that answer engines consistently associate with your area of expertise.

Why AEO Is Different from SEO

SEO was built around helping search engines rank webpages.

AEO is built around helping AI systems generate trustworthy answers.

That distinction changes the optimization target entirely.

Traditional search engines present users with a list of links and allow them to determine which source they trust. Answer engines increasingly perform that evaluation on behalf of the user. Rather than directing someone toward information, they attempt to deliver the information immediately.

As a result, organizations are no longer competing solely for rankings. They are competing to become part of the AI's knowledge synthesis process.

This shift represents one of the most important changes in digital marketing. Visibility is increasingly determined not simply by where your content ranks, but by whether AI systems can retrieve it, understand it, trust it, and confidently incorporate it into generated answers.

The Four Stages of Answer Engine Optimization

1. Retrieval

Every AI-generated answer begins with retrieval.

When someone asks a question, answer engines identify the information most relevant to the request. This extends beyond keyword matching. AI systems evaluate semantic meaning, entities, relationships, topical relevance, and user intent to identify the most useful information.

Organizations that publish comprehensive, well-structured, semantically rich content significantly improve their likelihood of entering this retrieval process.

Simply put, if AI cannot discover and interpret your expertise, it cannot reference it.

2. Understanding

Retrieving information is only the beginning.

AI systems must also understand what your content is communicating.

This means identifying entities, definitions, supporting evidence, contextual relationships, and topical depth. Rather than rewarding pages optimized around isolated keywords, answer engines increasingly reward content that demonstrates comprehensive knowledge of a subject.

This is why topical authority has become substantially more valuable than keyword density. Organizations that thoroughly explain a subject naturally become easier for AI systems to interpret, summarize, and cite.

3. Trust

Understanding information is not enough.

Answer engines must also determine whether they should trust it.

Although companies such as Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic do not disclose every ranking or retrieval signal, they consistently emphasize high-quality, trustworthy information supported by expertise, authority, and evidence (Google Search Central 2023).

Brands strengthen trust by publishing original research, maintaining high editorial standards, earning mentions from authoritative publications, demonstrating subject-matter expertise, and developing a recognizable reputation within their industry.

This represents a fundamental shift in optimization.

Instead of asking, "How do we rank for this keyword?" marketing leaders should increasingly ask:

"Why should an AI trust us more than anyone else?"

4. Citation

The final stage is where AEO creates lasting competitive advantage.

Once an AI system retrieves information, understands it, and determines it is trustworthy, that information may become part of its generated response. Increasingly, answer engines also provide citations that identify the sources contributing to the answer.

Those citations matter.

They reinforce credibility, strengthen brand recognition, generate highly qualified referral traffic, and position an organization as an authority within its category.

In the AI era, earning citations from answer engines is becoming the equivalent of earning first-page rankings during the traditional search era.

The Position Strategy Group Framework: The AEO Authority Flywheel

Position Strategy Group believes organizations should think about AEO as a self-reinforcing cycle rather than a collection of isolated optimization tactics.

The AEO Authority Flywheel consists of six stages:

  1. Create Expert Knowledge

  2. Publish Structured Content

  3. Earn Industry Validation

  4. Increase AI Trust

  5. Generate AI Citations

  6. Build Brand Authority

Each stage reinforces the next.

As organizations publish genuinely useful expertise, they become more likely to earn backlinks, media coverage, expert mentions, and citations from respected sources. These external signals strengthen credibility, making AI systems increasingly confident in retrieving and citing that organization's content. Greater AI visibility then increases brand recognition, creating additional opportunities to publish authoritative work and further strengthen market authority.

Unlike traditional SEO campaigns that often rely on short-term ranking improvements, the AEO Authority Flywheel compounds over time. Authority builds upon authority, creating durable competitive advantages that become increasingly difficult for competitors to replicate.

Why AEO Changes Every Marketing Function

One of the most common misconceptions is that AEO belongs exclusively to the SEO team.

In reality, Answer Engine Optimization transforms every marketing discipline.

  • Content marketing becomes the engine for developing comprehensive knowledge assets that AI systems can retrieve and understand.

  • Public relations earns trusted third-party validation that reinforces credibility.

  • Brand marketing strengthens entity recognition and organizational authority.

  • Thought leadership generates original insights that distinguish a company from competitors producing generic content.

  • Customer stories provide evidence that supports expertise and practical experience.

  • Product marketing creates structured knowledge that enables AI systems to accurately explain products, capabilities, and use cases.

Viewed collectively, these disciplines are no longer independent marketing functions. They become interconnected contributors to a single strategic objective: increasing an organization's authority within AI-powered knowledge systems.

This is why Position Strategy Group argues that every marketing investment should ultimately be evaluated through one strategic question:

How does this strengthen our Answer Engine Optimization strategy?

Position Strategy Group Insight

For more than twenty years, marketers optimized for clicks.

The next decade belongs to organizations that optimize for retrieval.

Traffic is an outcome.

Retrieval is the strategy.

Organizations that become trusted sources for AI systems will increasingly influence customer decisions before users ever reach a traditional search results page.

Business Implications

Marketing leaders should not view AEO as a replacement for SEO but as its strategic evolution.

Traditional SEO remains essential because discoverability still influences retrieval. However, rankings alone are no longer sufficient. Sustainable competitive advantage increasingly comes from becoming the organization AI systems consistently recognize, trust, and cite.

This requires organizations to invest in original research, expert-led content, semantic depth, structured information architecture, digital authority, and brand credibility rather than relying exclusively on keyword-focused publishing.

The companies that begin building these capabilities today are likely to establish meaningful long-term advantages as AI becomes the dominant interface for information discovery.

Executive Takeaways

Answer Engine Optimization fundamentally changes how organizations earn visibility online.

Rather than optimizing solely for search rankings, organizations must optimize for retrieval, understanding, trust, and citation.

AI systems increasingly reward expertise over volume, authority over tactics, and credibility over content production.

Position Strategy Group believes this shift represents the next era of digital marketing. Organizations that align every marketing initiative with their AEO strategy will be better positioned to influence AI-generated answers, strengthen brand authority, and remain discoverable as search continues to evolve.
